messages.author: 6dd12c407192b6b9
messages.subject: Binomial hierarchical model
parts:
I am trying to analyse a toy example that I have created in R. 

We can imagine the example as follows: we have followed 12 populations and measured a certain illness in the population. We are interested in the probability of being ill. 

Now we divide these populations in males and females which have their own probabilities in turn (we could in theory slice and dice the data differently). I would have intuitively expected that if a population is small its probability should be closer to the total population probability and vice versa. So this is why I believe a hierarchical model might be useful. 

I have coded such a model in stan, but I have some convergence issues. I would like to understand if my approach is appropriate and if so how I can modify my code so that it converges. 

I have generated my data as follows:

library(rstan)
set_cppo('fast')

set.seed(123)
population  <- rbinom(12,140,seq(0.1,0.9,length.out=12))
sick <- rbinom(12,population,0.01)

male <- rbinom(12,population,0.8)
female <- population - male
sick2 <- rbinom(12,sick,0.6)
sick1 <- sick - sick2

dat <- list(noexp=12,
            sub=3,
            pop = c(population,male,female),
            sick = c(sick,sick1,sick2),
            popind = rep(1:3,each=12))

fit <- stan(file="binom.stan",data=dat,iter=10000,chains=3,thin=10)

To analyse the data I have used the following model. 

data {
  int noexp;              // number of experiments 
  int sub;                // number of subpop
  int pop[sub*noexp];     // populations
  int sick[sub*noexp];    // sick
  int popind[sub*noexp];  // pop index
}

parameters {
  real<lower=0> tau;
  real eta[sub];
}

transformed parameters {
  real psick[sub];
  psick[1] <- inv_logit(100*eta[1]);
  for (j in 2:sub)
    psick[j] <- inv_logit(logit(psick[1]) + tau*eta[j]);
}

model {
  eta ~ normal(0,1);
  for (i in 1:noexp)  
    sick[i] ~ binomial(pop[i],psick[popind[i]]);
}

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Binomial hierarchical model
parts:
On May 25, 2014, at 4:10 PM, pehl...@gmail.com wrote:

>
> I am trying to analyse a toy example that I have created in R.
>
> We can imagine the example as follows: we have followed 12 populations and measured a certain illness in the population. We are interested in the probability of being ill.
>
> Now we divide these populations in males and females which have their own probabilities in turn (we could in theory slice and dice the data differently).

What'll happen in general is that we'll do a logistic regression, not directly
estimate probabilities for subpopulations.

> I would have intuitively expected that if a population is small its probability should be closer to the total population probability and vice versa. So this is why I believe a hierarchical model might be useful.

You mean you want to partially pool the male and female populations
using a hierarchical model? That you can do.

> I have coded such a model in stan, but I have some convergence issues. I would like to understand if my approach is appropriate and if so how I can modify my code so that it converges.
>
> I have generated my data as follows:
>
> library(rstan)
> set_cppo('fast')
>
> set.seed(123)
> population <- rbinom(12,140,seq(0.1,0.9,length.out=12))
> sick <- rbinom(12,population,0.01)
>
> male <- rbinom(12,population,0.8)
> female <- population - male
> sick2 <- rbinom(12,sick,0.6)
> sick1 <- sick - sick2
>
> dat <- list(noexp=12,
> sub=3,
> pop = c(population,male,female),
> sick = c(sick,sick1,sick2),
> popind = rep(1:3,each=12))
>
> fit <- stan(file="binom.stan",data=dat,iter=10000,chains=3,thin=10)

The trick is now to just write the model to match your
simulation, which your model below doesn't quite do. It
helps (me at least) to use the same variables in the
simulation as in the model, so they're easy to line up and
test for fit against the posterior.

>
> To analyse the data I have used the following model.
>
> data {
> int noexp; // number of experiments
> int sub; // number of subpop
> int pop[sub*noexp]; // populations
> int sick[sub*noexp]; // sick
> int popind[sub*noexp]; // pop index
> }
>

These all seem to be declared with the wrong
sizes given the way you loop over only parts of them below.

> parameters {
> real<lower=0> tau;
> real eta[sub];
> }
>
> transformed parameters {
> real psick[sub];
> psick[1] <- inv_logit(100*eta[1]);
> for (j in 2:sub)
> psick[j] <- inv_logit(logit(psick[1]) + tau*eta[j]);
> }
>
I don't understand why these all involve a psick[1] term.

> model {
> eta ~ normal(0,1);
> for (i in 1:noexp)
> sick[i] ~ binomial(pop[i],psick[popind[i]]);
> }

At this point, you just want to declare some parameters and
use a logit scaled predictor as the chance of success in
a call to binomial_logit(). That is, don't do your own inv_logit
transform --- it should just look like this:

sick[i] ~ binomial_logit(pop[i], logit(psick[1]) + tau*eta[j]);

Anyway, the usual way to do this would be to just write a hierarchical
logistic regression, which is here intercept-only because you don't have
other predictors in your simulation other than the population index
if I understand correctly.

- Bob
